title: Laser fragmentation in liquid - constructing a generic reaction map
authors: Anton Plech, Yogesh Pokhrel, Meike Tack, Matteo Levantino, Sven Reichenberger
abstract: Excitation of absorbing colloids in liquid by pulsed laser irradiation creates highly non-equilibrium states of matter that relax via defined pathways of thermal and non-thermal dissipation channels. The structural fingerprint of these channels can be probed by ultrafast {\it in situ} x-ray scattering methods and classified as a function of temporal delay of excitation excitation density, or specifically laser fluence. We study the example of photo-excitation of a gold colloid by picosecond laser pulses at the interband absorption band at 400 nm in water. By quantifying lattice temperature, crystalline fraction, particle sizes and the structural response of the water around the nanoparticles a reaction map is constructed that allows to pinpoint heating, particle melting, water bubble formation and finally particle fragmentation to form nanoclusters of predominant sizes of < 3 nm for applications in theranostics, photonics or catalysis.
summary: This research investigates how laser pulses induce structural changes, including heating, melting, and fragmentation, in metal colloids suspended in liquid. By using ultrafast x-ray scattering, the authors map out a generic reaction map that links the initial laser energy density to the final nanocluster size and structural state. This provides a fundamental understanding of energy dissipation pathways in non-equilibrium soft matter systems.
main_problem: To construct a generic reaction map describing the structural and chemical transitions that occur when absorbing colloids in liquid are excited by pulsed laser irradiation.
main_result: A generic reaction map is constructed that correlates final fragmentation products to the initial energy density and dynamics, unifying mechanisms from simple thermal heating to complex non-thermal fragmentation.
method: The study uses ultrafast in situ x-ray scattering (pump-probe) on gold colloids in water, analyzing time-resolved changes in lattice structure, particle size, and water density.
model_or_system: The physical system is the photo-excitation of gold colloids in water using picosecond laser pulses. The process is modeled as a relaxation from highly non-equilibrium states through defined thermal and non-thermal dissipation channels.
key_observables: Lattice temperature, crystalline fraction, particle sizes, water structural response, and scattering intensity changes ($\Delta I$) at various scattering vectors (q).
important_parameters: Laser fluence (F), temporal delay ($	au$), and the critical fluence threshold ($F_0$) marking the onset of melting/fragmentation.
main_assumptions: The relationship between thermal kinetics, liquid response, and particle fragmentation is assumed to be generic across different metals or liquids, and the fluence is treated as the fundamental control parameter.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate possible excitation pathways (thermal vs. non-thermal), size distributions of synthesized colloids, and the final generic reaction map correlating fluence/delay to fragmentation outcomes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the physical problem, detailing the experimental setup (pump-probe scattering), analyzing the quantitative changes in lattice structure and water state, and culminating in the construction and discussion of the generic reaction map.
why_interesting: The work deals with non-equilibrium dynamics, phase transitions (melting, fragmentation), and energy dissipation pathways in complex fluids, which are core topics in non-equilibrium statistical mechanics and open quantum systems.
